paragraphs.source_en: “No, no; if you understand the matter so reasonably, that is quite all right. You may throw the ball as much as you like; so long as you give notice and come in through the front gate, there is no problem. Well then, I hand these students back to you; please take them home with you. Ah, I am truly sorry to have troubled you to come all this way.” My master, in his usual fashion, made his customary courteous speech to the other party, beginning grandly and ending feebly. The ethics teacher led these warriors from Tanba’s Sasayama back to Rakuunkan through the front gate. Thus the great affair of which I spoke came, for the moment, to a close. If anyone laughs and says, “What? You call that a great affair?” let him laugh. It is merely that, for such a person, it is not a great affair. I am writing about my master’s great affairs, not about the great affairs of anyone else. If anyone jeers, saying, “This has a beginning but no end; it is the spent force of a strong bow,” I ask that jeerer to remember well: this is precisely my master’s distinguishing trait. And please remember also that it is just because he possesses this trait that my master becomes material for comic writing. If it is said that my master is a fool for taking fourteen- or fifteen-year-old brats as his opponents, then I agree that I too must be as foolish as my master; hence Omachi Keigetsu says of my master, “He has not yet escaped childishness.”

paragraphs.source_en: I have already narrated the minor incident, and now I have also related the major incident. Next I intend to describe the ripples that arose after the great affair, and thereby bring the whole course of the affair to its conclusion. Some readers may think that everything I have written is mere talk off the top of my head, random nonsense, but in fact I am not such a frivolous cat. Not only does every word and phrase of mine contain a great philosophy, but if those words and phrases are read in sequence, one will perceive that they are consistent from beginning to end and answer one another before and after. Even those who formerly took it for idle chatter and read it carelessly will, on reading it once again, at once change their view and feel that it is a most weighty instruction delivered by enlightened priests; therefore one must never adopt such rude postures as reading while lying down, stretching out one’s legs, or skimming five lines at a glance. It is said that whenever Liu Zongyuan read the prose of Han Tuizhi, he purified his hands with rose water; so with regard to my writings too, I ask you at least to buy the magazine with your own money, and never commit the disgraceful act of making do by borrowing what a friend has already finished reading. Although I myself call what I am about to relate the aftermath of the affair, if you suppose that because it is merely aftermath it must be dull and need not be read, you will regret it deeply. You must therefore read carefully to the very end.

paragraphs.source_en: On the day after the great affair occurred, I was seized with an elegant desire to take a walk and went out into the street. At that time, by the corner where one turns into the lane opposite, Mr. Kaneda and Mr. Tō of the Suzuki family were standing and talking; Kaneda was on his way home by rickshaw, while Suzuki had called when Kaneda was out and, on his way back, the two happened to meet. Lately the Kaneda mansion had ceased to be a novelty to me, so I seldom wandered in that direction, but seeing Kaneda this time made me somehow glad. It had also been a long time since I had seen Suzuki, so I decided to enjoy the honor of beholding him from the side. Having made up my mind thus, I ambled slowly up beside the two gentlemen, and naturally their conversation poured into my ears. This was not my eavesdropping; the fault could only lie with them for talking. Kaneda is a kind-hearted fellow who will even hire detectives to spy on my master’s movements, so even if I happened to listen respectfully to this gentleman’s conversation, there was no need to worry that he would be angry. If he were angry, that would mean he did not acknowledge that all things should be treated fairly, measure for measure. In any case, I heard the conversation of these two gentlemen. I did not listen because I wished to hear; rather, though I had no wish to hear at all, the conversation insisted on leaping into my ears.
